SN-P1.property: Storage resolution is unary: the root is a derived value, never an input.
SN-P1.ruling: HOLDS. The property is real and it is structural rather than a site list.
SN-P1.theAttackIRan: The tasking's sharpest question: can a root still be admitted by any path that does not go through the unary resolver? The answer is YES — and the subject says so itself, at admittedStorageRoot.role, which names exactly three selection sites: first-durable-write allocation, explicit adopt, and migration target reservation. So I tried to reach the SN-IR-01 defect through each of them.
whyEachSelectionSiteIsClosed: FIRST-DURABLE-WRITE ALLOCATION. The load-bearing fact is WHERE the authority record lives. I measured it: storageNamespace.inventoryPurgeMigration.migration.authorityRecordPath is '<userStateRoot>/opensip/storage-authority-v1/<ProjectId>.json' — user-state scoped, outside every admitted root, exactly one record per ProjectId. So selecting a decoy root for a ProjectId that already has a record does not get a fresh registry to win in: SN-P4 makes the generation-1 write create-new, a losing create-new is a losing compare-and-swap, and the operation refuses. Had the record been sited per-root, this attack would have succeeded and SN-P2/SN-P4 would both have been defeated. It is not, and the subject's reuse of the predecessor's own path is what makes the repair work.

EXPLICIT ADOPT. SN-P2 exit (a) permits a rebind only after the bound locator is proven ABSENT, and only at unchanged rootId and unchanged generation. A decoy root bears a DIFFERENT rootId, so it is not a locator rebind at all and exit (a) does not reach it.

MIGRATION TARGET RESERVATION. This is compare-and-swap against the expected generation and source root, and staged bytes are non-authoritative until it commits. It is the intended way to change roots. It leaves exactly one record naming exactly one root, so it produces no split.
SN-P1.residualCaseIProbedAndFoundHonestlyDiscl: A ProjectId whose user-state record is LOST while its durable evidence survives: a new first-durable-write can then legitimately win create-new at a different root, and the old namespace becomes an orphan. This is not silent — SN-P5 types it STORAGE_NAMESPACE_ORPHANED, refuses resolution on it and routes it to inventory's existing corrupt-orphan class, and SN-P5.whatItCloses names this exact case in the subject's own words: 'It also covers the case where the user-state authority record is lost while the durable evidence survives, which SN-P1 alone would silently treat as a project that has no storage.' The outcome is fail-closed with a typed signal, which is precisely what the predecessor lacked.
SN-P1.whatSeparatesThisFromTheReviewersProposa: The prior review proposed a comparison. A comparison has to be sited, and a site can be missed. SN-P1 removes the argument position instead, and — this is the part the subject under-sells — it does not stand alone. SN-P4 and SN-P5 are DURABLE-STATE rules, not API-shape rules: they bite on the filesystem, not on a call signature. An implementation that wrongly accepted a root argument would still lose create-new at SN-P4 and still trip STORAGE_NAMESPACE_ORPHANED at SN-P5. The defect is therefore unreachable by two independent routes, only one of which depends on the argument-position claim being honoured.
SN-P1.measurementConfirmed: The subject's differential-harness claim that predecessor resolution read the EMPTY SET of the authority record reproduces statically in the predecessor bytes: activeRootId appears exactly twice corpus-wide, in the field list and in the checker's assertion ABOUT that field list, and nowhere as a consumer. Under the effective contract activeRootId is the sole producer of the root half of every layout path, so it cannot fail to be read without the value failing to exist.

SN-P2.property: Root-instance uniqueness as an invariant of the authority-record set, evaluated at open time, with the locator only a presence probe.
SN-P2.ruling: HOLDS on substance. The refusal of the prior reviewer's criterion was RIGHT, but the ground stated for it MISCHARACTERISES that reviewer's text. Both halves of that finding matter.

adjudicationOfTheRefusal.whatTheSubjectSaysTheReviewerProposed: 'the reviewer's conflict criterion was "equal rootId, different canonical path". That re-promotes the path to a decision procedure one clause after demoting it.'
adjudicationOfTheRefusal.whatTheReviewerActuallyWrote: 'Resolving a ProjectId against a root whose rootId equals activeRootId but whose canonical path differs from activeRootCanonicalPath is a typed conflict, not an implicit rebind. Resolve it exactly as PROJECT-ID-V1 resolves its analogue: refuse implicitly, and require either (a) an explicit move/adopt after proving the old root is ABSENT, permitting one atomic locator rebind at unchanged generation, or (b) an explicit fork that re-allocates a fresh rootId into the copy. Two live roots bearing one rootId are refused and neither is selected.'
adjudicationOfTheRefusal.theMischaracterisation: The reviewer's path comparison is a TRIGGER, not a decision procedure. The reviewer's actual DECISION is liveness-based and says so twice — 'after proving the old root is ABSENT' and 'two live roots bearing one rootId are refused'. That is the same discriminator SN-P2 uses. The subject quotes only the trigger clause and attributes to it a dispositive role the reviewer's full sentence does not give it. This corpus's recorded failure mode is paraphrasing a document into saying what it did not say, and here the candidate does it to the review it answers.
whyTheRefusalIsNeverthelessCorrect: CONSISTENCY WITH THE DEMOTION. Under SN-P1 activeRootCanonicalPath is advisory and, by §6 law 8, an exact accelerator that may be stale. The reviewer's trigger fires 'typed conflict' on a benign move — one root, no conflict, merely a stale hint — and then has to rescue it through branch (a). SN-P2 never calls a stale locator a conflict; it calls it STORAGE_ROOT_LOCATOR_STALE. That is a genuine improvement, not a restatement.

EXPRESSIVENESS. A resolution-time comparison constrains only what is READ. A set invariant also constrains what may be WRITTEN, which is what licenses SN-P2's inexpressibility argument at all. The reviewer's formulation could not have carried that clause.

IT DID NOT DISCARD A SIMPLER CORRECT RULE. The reviewer's rule is not simpler — it is the same liveness discriminator with an extra path-difference gate in front of it that the advisory-path demotion then has to undo.

attacksIRanAgainstTheInvariant: COPY: root at /a bearing rootId X copied to /b. Records bind X to /a; /a is PRESENT and bears X; /b differs. STORAGE_ROOT_COLLISION. Correct.

MOVE: /a renamed to /b. Records bind X to /a; /a is ABSENT. STORAGE_ROOT_LOCATOR_STALE, then one rebind under explicit adopt. Correct, and it discriminates the genuine move from the copy — a rule refusing both would be safe and useless.

ORDER INVERSION: admit the copy FIRST while the original is unmounted, rebind to it, then remount and admit the original. The invariant is symmetric: the original now differs from the bound locator, which is PRESENT and bears X, so it trips COLLISION. No ordering I tried lets both roots become live and bound.

MANY PROJECTS ONE ROOT: the predecessor explicitly permits this at admittedStorageRoot.notProjectExclusive. N records may all bind X to the same locator; the relation is still a function. No false collision.
SN-P2.wherePrecisionIsOwedAndIsNotGiven: See nonBlockingObservations SNV4R-NB-02. SN-P2 exit (a) says 'one atomic locator rebind', but with N projects on one root there are N records each carrying activeRootCanonicalPath, so a root move is N rebinds. A crash mid-rebind durably realises one rootId at two recorded locators — the very state the inexpressibility clause says cannot be written. The outcome is nonetheless safe, because each un-rebound record independently probes an ABSENT locator and reports LOCATOR_STALE, so the state self-heals. The rule is sound; the inexpressibility prose overstates it by one notch.

SN-P3.property: One device across the layout-derived rename operand set, stated once at pathSafety.resolution, retyping rather than extending pathSafety.unsupported.
SN-P3.ruling: HOLDS for the rename property it exists to establish. One unstated scope bound, recorded as SNV4R-NB-01.
SN-P3.theRetypingIsReal: I checked the claim that no predicate was added. pathSafety.unsupported's predicate list is unchanged between predecessor and effective contract — the only edit is 'Refuse a filesystem lacking...' becoming 'Refuse an operand lacking...', plus the sentence explaining that the domain of each predicate is the operands of the operation. Atomic rename genuinely is a capability of an ordered (source, target) pair rather than of a filesystem, so a cross-device pair lacks it as an instance of the existing rule. This is a correct retyping and not a disguised eighth entry.
SN-P3.derivedOperandPairsAreComplete: I re-derived the rename operand set from the predecessor's layout independently of the subject's declaration. The layout defines exactly three whole-namespace renames — purge commit (projectNamespace to purgeQuarantine), migration install (migrationStaging to projectNamespace), migration source retirement (projectNamespace to migrationRetirement) — and the only other atomic replace in the subtree is the authority record, which the predecessor already sites 'on the single user-state filesystem'. The subject's three declared pairs are exactly that set. There is no fourth.

executedOnRealHardware.standard: The author built a real 12 MiB HFS+ nested mount and got errno 18. I met that standard rather than arguing.
executedOnRealHardware.setup: A 12 MiB HFS+ disk image created with hdiutil and attached at projects/<ProjectId> inside a scratch tree, giving a genuine second device identity beneath an otherwise valid root. Measured st_dev: root 16777234, projects/ 16777234, quarantine/ 16777234, control/ 16777234, projects/P1 16777240.
executedOnRealHardware.testA_mountAtTheRenamedDirectory: Moving marker written and fsynced inside the canonical namespace, then rename of projects/P1 into quarantine/purge/P1/pg1/namespace. Result: errno=18 EXDEV, 'Cross-device link'. This reproduces the author's measurement exactly.

SN-P3.doesTestBDefeatSNP3: No, and I checked this carefully because it was my best shot. SN-P3's statement scopes the scan to 'the root itself, projects/, control/, quarantine/ and every directory beneath projects/ and quarantine/'. 'Every directory beneath projects/' is recursive, so projects/<ProjectId>/data is inside the scan and the Test B root is refused at admission with STORAGE_ROOT_NOT_ONE_DEVICE before any user-derived durable write. Both configurations I built are caught. I note that blockerDisposition's gloss 'it must range one level below projects/' reads, in isolation, like a shallower scope than the normative statement grants; the normative statement is the one that governs and it is the recursive one.

unaryResolverObjection.theObjection: A specification cannot delete an argument position in someone else's implementation, so SN-P1 is still just a rule, and rules get missed. The author concedes this and scopes it: at the specification level the bad state is inexpressible; at the implementation level conformance is a runtime property no instrument here can observe, and rootBinding.observabilityBoundary says so.
unaryResolverObjection.ruling: SUFFICIENT — this is not a paper seal. But the artifact's own word 'inexpressible' overstates by one notch, and the artifact contains its own correction.
whyItIsNotAPaperSeal: A paper seal is an unenforced claim presented as enforced. This is an unenforced claim presented AS unenforced, with the boundary named at rootBinding.observabilityBoundary, a falsification condition written down, and the disclosure confirmed by a measurement the author reported AGAINST ITS OWN INTEREST. I reproduced that measurement and it is worse than the author states: not merely rootBinding but the ENTIRE 13-operation derivation leaves check-threat-claims.py output byte-identical. The author disclosed the direction of the defect accurately and did not soften it.

The scoping is the correct one. IMPLEMENTER-BLUEPRINT.md §5.1's E-NS-1 records a failure BY OMISSION — an implementer reaches for root selection, root identity validation, authority-record creation and the rename's same-device precondition and cannot build them. All four are now buildable. That is the recorded defect, and it is repaired.

The claim does not rest on the argument-position assertion alone. As recorded under SN-P1 above, SN-P4 and SN-P5 are durable-state rules that catch the same defect on the filesystem regardless of what an implementation's call signature accepts. An implementer who ignores SN-P1 entirely still cannot reach two live namespaces for one ProjectId without also violating SN-P4's create-new and SN-P5's orphan refusal. The subject defends SN-P1 on its own terms and never makes this argument; it is the strongest defence available to it and it is left on the table.
unaryResolverObjection.whereTheWordOverstates: storageNamespace.authority says a disagreeing root 'cannot be stated', and SN-P2 carries an 'inexpressibility' clause. At the specification level that is true only of a CONFORMING host. The artifact knows this — STORAGE_ROOT_CALLER_SUPPLIED exists precisely because the state is expressible in a non-conforming one, and its definition says so: 'this outcome exists to be unreachable in a conforming host and detectable in a non-conforming one.' So the honest reading is present in the artifact's own bytes one section away from the overstatement. I record this as a precision matter, not a defect: minting a detector for the state you have just called inexpressible is the behaviour of a specification that expects to be violated, which is the right expectation.
unaryResolverObjection.theResidualThatRemains: Conformance is a G14-class runtime property and no instrument in this corpus can observe it. Nothing in this review changes that, and the subject does not claim otherwise.

isTheGreenRunVACUOUS.question: A green T13 is only evidence if T13 would have fired had the derivation broken something. §7.4 forbids reading an exit code as evidence a guard fired; the converse trap is reading a green as evidence a guard was satisfied when it checks nothing.

isTheGreenRunVACUOUS.conclusion: 6 of 6 caught, and every one is REJECTED-BY-POSITION in §7.4's taxonomy — the finding names the mutated leaf — not REJECTED-COLLATERAL. T13 is a live instrument over the parts this candidate does not change, and the subject's whyItWasDesignedToStayGreen is an accurate account of a real constraint the twelve prose values were written to satisfy.

areTheSixSufficient.ruling: NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT. They bind structure well and semantics not at all.
areTheSixSufficient.whatTheyDoBind: Assertion 4 is the strongest of the six and is genuinely good: re-deriving derivedOperandPairs from layout rather than reading them from the artifact is the same discipline the existing T13 applies to fixture paths, and it would catch a declared operand pair the layout does not produce. Assertion 5 binds the row counts to live recomputation, which is the §7.2.2 rule applied correctly. Assertions 2 and 3 close the outcome vocabulary and the vector-to-property references. Assertion 6 carries §7.5 and §6 law 18 forward, and correctly names rootBinding.schemaVersion and the boolean valid fields as the exact-type positions.
areTheSixSufficient.theGap: Assertion 1 requires only that each of SN-P1..SN-P5 'carries a non-empty statement'. There is no required-substring test on any of the five property statements — and required-substring tests over prose are precisely the technique the pinned T13 uses over the predecessor, which I demonstrated above is live and position-naming. A successor checker carrying exactly these six would exit 0 on a rootBinding whose five statements had been replaced with placeholders. That is a checker that would catch the STRUCTURE of the repair regressing but not its CONTENT being gutted, which is the failure mode the three original blockers were.
areTheSixSufficient.fairnessToTheAuthor: The subject's own heading is 'what a successor checker MUST add', which states a floor and not a completeness claim, so this is not an overclaim by the subject. But the tasking asked whether the six are sufficient to catch the three defects, and measured against that question the answer is no. Recorded as SNV4R-NB-03 and owed to SNV4-RES-01 before a coordinator commissions the checker.

isAnUnenforcedRepairACCEPTABLEFORACANDID.ruling: YES, on these specific facts, with the residual sharpened.
reasons: The alternative was verified by execution to be impossible: fixtures in storageNamespace.fixtures break the pinned checker on application.

The lane is forbidden to write a checker, and IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §7.6 records that editing one is not merely unwise but self-defeating — two checkers self-pin and cannot be repaired in place at all.
The candidate binds nothing, asserts no verdict on itself, and carries the gap as SNV4-RES-01 with the coordinator named as owner.
The disclosure is measured rather than asserted, and the measurement runs against the author's own interest.

An unenforced repair would NOT be acceptable for an APPLIED or SEALED artifact, and nothing in this review should be read as permitting that. Application without a successor checker leaves rootBinding as specification text, which is exactly what its own fixtures.enforcementDisclosure says.

section46NonDisturbance.question: Does the SN-P3 repair disturb IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §4.6's DISCHARGED purge-semantics item?
section46NonDisturbance.ruling: NO. I attempted the subject's own falsification and could not meet it. The non-disturbance is structural, not incidental.
section46NonDisturbance.theFalsificationIAttempted: Exhibit a purge whose availability semantics differ because its root spans two devices.
whyItCannotBeMet: effective_capability's signature takes (sealedCapability, units, availabilityRecords) and no root, path or device parameter. Its forbiddenInputs list has eleven members and physicalLocators is one of them — physical location is EXPLICITLY banned from the derivation, not merely absent from it.

An AST walk of the derivation's function closure reads exactly ten field names: atSequence, objectRefs, objectStates, projectId, recordCasRef, recordKind, requiredForCapability, state, toState, unitId. No device, path, filesystem, root, mount, atomicity or commit-versus-refusal flag. A counterexample would require the derivation to read a field it provably never reads.
Executed against the real v22 closure: device identity injected into every input position, split across two devices at all 20 possible split points. 0 of 20 results differed from baseline.

The actual EXDEV durable state modelled through the derivation — journal PREPARED, canonical present, nothing unlinked, no ledger append — returns replayable with refusal NONE, byte-identical to baseline. That is semantically correct: the purge did not happen, so the evidence is still fully available.

The domain of the discharge is 'purges that occur', not 'projects that exist'. The obligation text is 'State how purge changes current evidence availability without rewriting the sealed Run', which is conditioned on a purge occurring. A root refused at admission never produces a sealed Run, so the function is never invoked.
section46NonDisturbance.measuredNonOverlapReproduced: retention-tiers.v24.json contains 0 occurrences of 'storageNamespace' and check-retention-custody-v24.py contains 0. Both reproduce exactly. Also measured 0 for EXDEV, st_dev, mount, rootId and 'admitted root' in both. The single 'device' hit in Part B is consentPromise.notGuaranteed[5], 'Cryptographic erasure of the raw bytes on the underlying device' — a disclaimer, not a semantics input.
twoFindingsThatGoBEYONDWhatTheSubjectArg: The PREDECESSOR's rules, not SN-P3, were the configuration that could put a durable state on disk which Part B's closed four-member availability lattice (AVAILABLE, OUTAGE, MISSING-DEPENDENCY, PURGED) has no member for. SN-P3 eliminates that state. It moves the world TOWARD Part B's model, not away from it.

Part B has already carved out the failed-purge case itself. consentPromise.notGuaranteed[4] reads 'Any timing, atomicity or crash-safety property. Crash-safe purge is operability G5 against a built storage engine and is not demonstrated here.' A rename returning EXDEV IS an atomicity failure, already assigned to G5. SN-P3 therefore operates entirely inside a region Part B explicitly declined to cover.
section46NonDisturbance.theOneResidualStatedFairly: SN-P3 is a genuine DOMAIN RESTRICTION — it removes (root, project) pairs that would previously have existed and hosted purges. Restricting the domain of a universally quantified claim cannot falsify that claim, which is why the discharge survives. It would matter only if §4.6's discharge were a coverage claim ('purge works on all roots'). It is not: it is a read-time semantics claim over one in-memory closure, and RT23-B-RES-03 declares executedAgainstARealStore: 0. On the bytes as written, the coverage reading is not available. If a reviewer nonetheless takes it, §8's 'detected conflict with a binding artifact' limb is the right route — and I note the subject's citation of §8 for this purpose is a correct pointer even though §8 contains no 'DISCHARGED' language of its own.
section46NonDisturbance.escalation: None required. No §8 escalation is raised by this review.

attacksAttemptedAndTheirOutcomes.attack: Exhibit a seventh row in the purge crash-recovery table.
attacksAttemptedAndTheirOutcomes.method: Both real nested-mount configurations were driven to their durable end states and each was matched against the closed 6-row table.
attacksAttemptedAndTheirOutcomes.outcome: FAILED — no seventh row could be exhibited.
detail: Test A (EXDEV): moving marker durable, rename refused, nothing persisted. Durable tuple PREPARED|canonical-present|quarantine-absent. That is ROW 1, 'resume-atomic-quarantine'. Covered.
Test B (rename succeeded with the mount relocated): durable tuple PREPARED|canonical-absent|quarantine-present-matching-marker. That is ROW 2, 'reconcile-rename-gap'. Covered.

Test B continued into the delete phase: rmdir of the still-mounted directory returns errno=16 EBUSY, so the tuple is DELETE_IN_PROGRESS|canonical-absent|quarantine-present. That is ROW 4, 'resume-idempotent-delete', which loops. A non-terminating loop is not a new durable state and forces no row.

The closure test itself is the right one. The table's domain is durable state, purge.reachableDurableNonterminalStates has exactly 4 members and purge.states exactly 5, and no configuration I built persists a state outside that set. An operation that refuses without persisting a transition leaves the durable state identical to the state before it and therefore contributes no point to the domain. Purge stays 6 rows, migration stays 10.

attacksAttemptedAndTheirOutcomes.attack: Defeat the EXDEV/EBUSY refinement — show that binding to one errno would have been adequate, or that the subject binds to one.
attacksAttemptedAndTheirOutcomes.outcome: FAILED, and the subject's position is stronger than it claims.
detail: The subject does NOT bind to an errno. SN-P3's statement is a device-identity and mount-point property; the errnos appear only as measured examples in blockerDisposition and renameAtomicity.measuredRatherThanArgued. Verified by reading the property text.

The claim that binding to one errno would have been wrong is TRUE and I found a third behaviour the subject does not name. On this host: mount AT the renamed directory gives EXDEV(18); mount BENEATH gives SILENT SUCCESS with the mount relocated; rmdir of a mount point gives EBUSY(16). macOS man 2 rename documents EXDEV and does not document EBUSY, whereas Linux rename(2) documents EBUSY for a directory in use as a mount point — so the platform dependence the subject asserts is real.

Three distinct behaviours across configurations and platforms is a stronger argument for not binding to an errno than the two the subject gives. Its characterisation of the alternative as 'the §6 law 18 mistake in another register' is apt: law 18's own closing sentence is 'The law binds the property, not the language', and an errno spelling is language.

attacksAttemptedAndTheirOutcomes.attack: Admit a root by a path that does not go through the unary resolver.

nonBlockingObservations.title: SN-P3's stated scan scope does not reach the directories that actually hold the purge journal, although whyControlIsInScope gives protecting that journal as the reason control/ is in scope at all.
nonBlockingObservations.quote: SN-P3.statement: 'A storage root is admitted only if the root itself, projects/, control/, quarantine/ and every directory beneath projects/ and quarantine/ report one device identity, and no path within that scope is a mount point.'
nonBlockingObservations.theGap: The scanned set is {root, projects/, control/, quarantine/} union {every directory beneath projects/} union {every directory beneath quarantine/}. Recursion is granted to projects/ and quarantine/ and withheld from control/. But layout.purgeJournal is '<admittedStorageRoot>/control/purge/<ProjectId>/<purgeId>.v1.json', so the journal sits beneath control/purge/<ProjectId>/ — two levels below control/ and outside the stated scope. A mount at control/purge/ puts the journal on a different device from the namespace it describes, which is the exact condition whyControlIsInScope calls 'a worse defect than the rename failure itself'.
whyItIsNotBlocking: SN-P3's statement is an 'only if' — a necessary condition — and claims no sufficiency, so it does not say anything false. This is an omission, in the same class as the bounds the subject DOES state.

The rename operand set, which is what SN-IR-03 was actually about, is fully covered: all three derived operand pairs have both endpoints under projects/ or quarantine/, both of which are scanned recursively. The repair of the named blocker is complete.

The consequence is fail-closed and reportable rather than silent: a journal lost to an unmounted device leaves a quarantined namespace that inventory.root already separates into its corrupt-orphan class.
nonBlockingObservations.whyItStillMatters: The subject is otherwise scrupulous about stating the bounds of this scan — renameAtomicity.reachOfTheAdmissionScan explicitly discloses the file-level bind mount and the post-admission mount. This bound is of the same kind and is not disclosed, which is an asymmetry in a discipline the artifact otherwise maintains well.
nonBlockingObservations.suggestedDisposition: Sharpen in a successor: either extend the recursion to control/, or state the bound at reachOfTheAdmissionScan alongside the two already there. Either resolves it; the second is cheaper and is consistent with admissionCost.

nonBlockingObservations.title: SN-P2's 'one atomic locator rebind' and its inexpressibility clause do not account for a root shared by many projects, where a move requires N rebinds and a crash between them durably writes the state the clause says cannot be written.
nonBlockingObservations.quote: SN-P2.inexpressibility: 'The record set cannot record the ambiguity: writing the second, disagreeing binding IS the invariant violation. "One rootId at two live roots" has no representation it could later be resolved from, so there is no ambiguous durable state for a recovery rule to arbitrate.'
nonBlockingObservations.theGap: authorityRecordPath is '<userStateRoot>/opensip/storage-authority-v1/<ProjectId>.json' — one file per ProjectId — and admittedStorageRoot.notProjectExclusive explicitly permits many projects under one root. So N projects on one root means N records each carrying activeRootCanonicalPath. A root move must rebind all N. Those are N separate atomic file replaces, not one, and a crash after k of them leaves one rootId recorded at two different canonical locators — precisely the 'second, disagreeing binding'.
nonBlockingObservations.whyItIsNotBlocking: The outcome is safe and self-healing under the rules as stated. The k rebound records name a locator that is PRESENT; the N-k stale ones name a locator that is ABSENT and therefore each independently reports STORAGE_ROOT_LOCATOR_STALE and is rebound on next open. No COLLISION is falsely raised, because collision requires two PRESENT locators and a move leaves one. The invariant is momentarily violated in the record set and is restored by the same presence probe that enforces it.
nonBlockingObservations.whatIsOwed: The word 'one' in exit (a), and the inexpressibility clause, are true of the single-project case and overstated for the many-project case the predecessor permits. An implementer must decide whether adopt rebinds every record naming that rootId or only the one being resolved; both choices are consistent with the stated rules and both are safe, so this is a benign decision rather than an unbuildable fork — which is why it is graded non-blocking rather than blocking.

nonBlockingObservations.title: The six assertions checkerImpact requires of a successor checker bind the structure of rootBinding but not the content of its five property statements, and would exit 0 on a rootBinding gutted to placeholders.
nonBlockingObservations.quote: checkerImpact.whatASuccessorCheckerMUSTaddBeforeTheNewMaterialIsMECHANICALLYbound[0]: 'storageNamespace.rootBinding.properties has exactly the closed key set {SN-P1, SN-P2, SN-P3, SN-P4, SN-P5} and each member carries a non-empty statement.'
nonBlockingObservations.theGap: Non-emptiness is the only content test in the six. There is no required-substring assertion on any of SN-P1..SN-P5 — yet required-substring tests over prose are exactly how the pinned T13 binds the predecessor's semantics, and I demonstrated by mutation that this technique is live and position-naming in check-threat-claims.py. A successor checker carrying precisely these six would catch the structure regressing and would not catch the content being emptied, which is the shape the three original blockers had.
nonBlockingObservations.whyItIsNotBlocking: The subject's own heading is 'what a successor checker MUST add', which states a floor rather than claiming completeness, and the gap is already owned by SNV4-RES-01 with the coordinator named. The candidate does not overclaim here.
nonBlockingObservations.suggestedDisposition: Before a coordinator commissions the successor checker, add a seventh assertion binding each of the five property statements to its load-bearing substrings, on the model of the existing T13 tests over purpose, rootContents, authorityRecordRule and inventory.userAuthority.

reviewerStatement: I tried to reject this and could not. The three properties are not prose repairs: SN-P1 is backed by two durable-state rules that catch the same defect on the filesystem even if the argument-position claim is ignored, SN-P2 is a set invariant sited on a registry the predecessor already declared at a path outside every admitted root, and SN-P3 caught both real nested-mount configurations I built to defeat it. Every measurement the subject declares was reproduced independently, including the three subtree serialisations, the 0-error derivation resolution, the byte-identity of all 21 closed collections, the EXDEV errno on real hardware, and the disclosure that deleting rootBinding changes no checker output — which is worse than the subject says, since the entire derivation changes no checker output, and the subject reported the direction of that correctly and against its own interest. I could exhibit neither a seventh recovery row nor a §4.6 conflict. The five things I did find are real and none of them reopens a blocker: the clearest are that SN-P3's scan scope does not reach the purge journal's own directories although the artifact gives protecting that journal as the reason control/ is in scope, and that the six successor-checker assertions bind rootBinding's structure without binding its content. Both are recorded above with the grading argument written out, so a coordinator who disagrees with the grade can act on the finding without having to reconstruct it. This review changes no status, disposition, verdict or seal, touches no [UNSET], and does not clear TM.
